To use the subjunctive after negated verbs of opinion (no creo que, no pienso que).

8 December, Barajas airport in Madrid. Ecaterina and Ana have just landed. Marta is waiting for them at the arrivals gate, with a sign on which she has written “Ecaterina” in big letters.
Ana, wait a moment. I can’t go out yet. My legs are shaking.
It’s normal for you to be nervous. You’ve waited forty years for this moment.
It’s not that I’m afraid, it’s that I don’t know what I’m going to say. Besides, I don’t think he’ll recognise me today.
Well, I think he will. It’s obvious he remembers you: he recognised you on the video call.
(coming up to them) Ecaterina? How wonderful! I can’t believe you’re finally here.
Marta… you look just like your grandfather at your age. The same glasses.
Everyone says that. My grandfather is at home. Today is a good day: he woke up asking for you.
You see? It’s natural that he remembers. Some things aren’t forgotten.
The good thing is that I don’t have time to be afraid any more. Let’s go.
I think it’s very good that you’re coming straight there. He’s been sitting by the window since seven, with a book on his knees.
“me tiemblan las piernas” = my legs are shaking
«Yo creo que SÍ» / «Yo creo que NO»: the stress falls on the last word, which closes the opinion. «Pues…» at the start softens the tone.
ba-RA-jas: the “j” is strongly aspirated, like an “h” from the throat.
No me parece que esté cansado.
A typical mistake: «Creo que sea…» (calqued on Romanian or Italian). Correct: «Creo que es…». And the other way round: «No creo que es…» → «No creo que sea…».
In negative questions expecting a “yes”, the indicative can be used: «¿No crees que es mejor así?» (Don’t you think it’s better this way? = I think it is).

Ask yourself: am I stating a fact (indicative) or judging and evaluating it (subjunctive)? And when negated, even certainties switch to the subjunctive: «No es cierto que sea así».
3. Me parece que / me parece bien que
I think it’s going to rain. (opinion → indicative)
I think it’s good that you’re coming straight there. (judgement → subjunctive)
I think it’s awful that they didn’t let you know.
4. “No es que… sino que…” and “lo bueno es que…”
It’s not that I don’t want to go, it’s that I can’t.
The good thing is that I don’t have time to be afraid any more.
The bad thing is that the flight leaves very early.
The rejected part (no es que) is in the subjunctive; the true part (sino que / es que) is in the indicative. “Lo bueno / lo malo / lo peor es que” + indicative (you’re stating a fact).
Es una pena que no ha venido.
Es una pena que no vendrá.

Two readers’ letters in a newspaper, with opposing opinions. Notice the verb moods.

Dear Editor: it is obvious that many emigrants dream of returning to their country. But I don’t think it’s a good idea to go back after so many years. It’s natural that the city has changed and that friends have left. The bad thing is that you no longer recognise the place where you were born. (Carmen R., Valencia)

Dear Editor: I don’t agree with Señora Carmen’s letter. It’s not that the past comes back, but that we come back to it with different eyes. I find it sad that anyone should give up going back out of fear of what they will find. (Julián M., Bucharest)
I think we all have a place we return to in our dreams. The good thing is that, sometimes, that place is waiting for us too. (Julián M., Bucharest)
Que no es buena idea volver después de muchos años
Que alguien renuncie a regresar por miedo

Madrid was lit up for Christmas. From the taxi, Ecaterina looked at the streets without saying anything: the Gran Vía full of lights, people with shopping bags, roast chestnut stalls on the corners. Ana asked her if the city had changed much. Ecaterina took a while to answer. Then she said she didn’t think it had changed that much. It was she who had changed.

In the taxi, Marta told them about her mother. Pilar lived in Seville, where she worked as a paediatrician, and came to Madrid one weekend a month. It was she who, at first, had doubted the story in the novel. She found it impossible that her father, such a reserved man, could have lived through a love like that without ever telling her. “Now she says it’s only natural he didn’t tell,” Marta explained. “That some loves are kept the way good books are kept: on the top shelf, so that nobody touches them.”

Marta’s flat was on the third floor, with no lift, on the calle del Prado, two hundred metres from the old bookshop. Ecaterina climbed the stairs very slowly, holding on to Ana’s arm, stopping on every landing. On the second one she stopped completely. She said she wasn’t sure she could go on. Marta, who was ahead, turned round and told her gently that it was normal to be afraid, but that her grandfather had been climbing those stairs in his memory for forty years.

In the hallway, hanging on the wall, there was a wooden sign painted green, its letters half worn away by time: “Librería La Lámpara”. Ecaterina stopped in front of it and touched it with her fingertips. Marta told her that her grandfather had brought it home the day the shop closed, in 1994, and had never allowed anyone to take it down. “He used to say that as long as the sign was hanging, the bookshop hadn’t completely closed.”

The living-room door was ajar. From the hallway you could see a window with a white curtain, an armchair and, in the armchair, in profile, a very thin man with a blanket over his legs. He had a book on his knees, held the way you hold a plate of hot soup, with his left hand open underneath. He was looking out of the window.

Ecaterina stayed in the doorway. Ana thought she was going to say something, to call him by his name. But she didn’t. Instead, she did something nobody expected: she took off her coat, left it on a chair, walked slowly to the armchair and, without a word, took the book out of his hands, closed it and looked at the cover. It was an old book with worn corners. Rayuela (Hopscotch). Julio Cortázar.

Andrés turned his head very slowly. He looked at her for a long time. Ana held her breath. Marta, beside her, covered her mouth with her hand. Then a smile appeared on Andrés’s face, small at first, then enormous, a smile that changed his whole face and took twenty years off him at a stroke.
“About time,” he said. “I can’t believe it took you so long to come and get it. You left it on the counter in 1987. I’ve kept it for you.”

Ecaterina sat down on a chair beside the armchair, with the book in her lap. For a while they didn’t speak. They just looked at each other, like two people trying to recognise in an old face the young face they once knew. Then Andrés took her hand. His skin was as thin as the paper of an old book. Ecaterina told him she didn’t believe he had really waited for her all that time. He answered that it wasn’t that he had waited for her, but that he had never stopped, which was different.

Ana and Marta slipped quietly into the kitchen and closed the door. Marta made coffee with trembling hands. She told Ana that her grandfather hadn’t talked so much for weeks, and that the doctor had told her not to get her hopes up, that the good days were getting rarer and rarer. “It’s a pity we didn’t find you sooner,” she said. Ana replied that what mattered wasn’t when, but that it had happened.

Half an hour later, Ecaterina called them. Her eyes were red, but she was calm. She told them she wanted to do something before Andrés got tired, and asked them to stay. She took the yellowed envelope out of her bag. Andrés looked at it without understanding. Ecaterina explained that it was the letter she had written that night in 1987, in front of the closed door of the bookshop, and had never managed to post.
“It’s yours,” she said. “It’s forty years late, but it’s arrived. Do you want me to read it to you?”

Andrés nodded. Ecaterina put on her glasses, carefully unfolded the sheet, because the paper was tearing along the folds, and read aloud, slowly, with the voice of an eighty-year-old woman and the words of a woman of forty-two.

“Andrés: I’m leaving tomorrow. My mother is ill and I have to go back. I don’t know if I will ever be able to come back. It’s not that I don’t want to stay, it’s that they won’t let me choose. I’m not asking you to wait for me. That would be unfair. I’m only asking you not to forget me completely. And if one day a foreign woman walks into your bookshop looking for Cortázar, don’t sell her what she’s looking for. Give her another book, the way you did with me. Maybe then she’ll stay for ten years too. E.”

When she had finished, nobody said anything. Outside in the street, a busker was playing a Christmas carol on an accordion. Andrés held out his hand and Ecaterina gave him the letter. He held it for a moment, as if it weighed a great deal, and then put it inside Rayuela, between two pages, very carefully, the way you keep a pressed flower.
“I didn’t forget you completely,” he said at last. “I think it’s right that you should know. I’ve forgotten many other things. Lately I even forget my granddaughter’s name. But not that.”

The next afternoon they did something Andrés had been asking for for weeks and the doctor didn’t entirely approve of: they took him in his wheelchair through the streets of the Barrio de las Letras to the San Ginés chocolate shop. Marta pushed the chair. Ecaterina walked beside him, with her stick. Ana walked behind, taking photos for Costel, who asked for them every ten minutes from a car park in Poland.

They passed the old bookshop. It was now a clothes shop, with coloured lights in the window. Andrés asked them to stop for a moment. He looked at the front of the shop in silence. Ecaterina asked him if it made him sad. He answered no, that what matters about a bookshop isn’t the walls, but what people take home with them. And he winked at Ecaterina, who had Rayuela in her bag.

At San Ginés they ordered four hot chocolates with churros. Andrés got chocolate on his blanket and laughed like a child. Ecaterina, who hadn’t tasted it for forty years, said it was the best chocolate in the world, and that she didn’t think anywhere else made it the same. Andrés told her it was obvious they didn’t, because he wasn’t anywhere else.

That night, in the small guesthouse on the calle de las Huertas where they were staying, Ana and Ecaterina talked until late. Ana asked her if she regretted anything. Ecaterina thought about the answer for a long time. Then she said she didn’t think there was any point in regretting things at eighty. That it was obvious she had lost a lot of time, but the good thing was she still had a little left. And she intended to use it well.

Before falling asleep, Ecaterina asked Ana not to forget Mihai’s chorizo. Ana laughed and told her she had already bought it that morning at the San Miguel market, along with some turrón for Elena and a fan for Rosa Elena, identical to Grandma Carmen’s. Ecaterina remarked that she thought that was very good, because in that family, apparently, fans and frying pans were handed down like rings.

They stayed in Madrid for four days. Some were good and some not so good. On the third day, Andrés didn’t recognise anyone and spent the morning calling Ecaterina “Pilar”. She didn’t correct him. She read him chapters of Rayuela aloud for hours, although he didn’t seem to be listening. In the evening, suddenly, Andrés said to her: “You read that part better than in 1983.” And he was himself again for a whole hour.

On the last day, at the door of the flat, Ecaterina did what she hadn’t done in 1987: she said goodbye. She knelt beside the armchair, with great difficulty, kissed him on the forehead and promised she would come back in the spring. Andrés told her he thought that was a very good idea, but that this time she shouldn’t take forty years, because he was no longer up to such long waits.

On the plane home, Ecaterina fell asleep with Rayuela on her knees, her left hand open underneath it, like a tray. Ana watched her the whole flight. At one point, over the Alps, Ecaterina smiled in her sleep. Ana thought it had all been worth it: the journey, the stairs, the forty years. And she took out her phone to send Costel the last photo.
“no le parecía que hubiera cambiado” = she didn’t think it had changed
“no os hubiéramos encontrado” = we hadn’t found you
“no creía que sirviera de nada” = she didn’t think there was any point

Le quitó el libro a Andrés y dijo «Esto es mío»

Ana, I’ve seen all the photos. It’s incredible that a man of nearly ninety can smile like that. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a smile like it.
It’s not that I’m sentimental, it’s that I’ve been following this story from my lorry for three months. It’s normal for me to get emotional, isn’t it?
The good thing is that in spring I have a trip to Portugal. I think Madrid is on my way.
